body_text: Helios Technologies’ Electronics Segment Expands Support Across Briggs & Stratton Ecosystem July 14, 2026 9:00am EDT Download as PDF SARASOTA, Fla.--(BUSINESS WIRE)-- Helios Technologies, Inc. (NYSE: HLIO) (“Helios” or the “Company”), a global leader in highly engineered motion control and electronic controls technology, today announced that two businesses within its Electronics Segment— i3 Product Development (“i3PD”) and Enovation Controls (“Enovation”)—are supporting the off-highway equipment industry through separate commercial relationships with Briggs & Stratton . While each relationship serves a distinct role, together they highlight the breadth of engineering, systems integration, and electronic control capabilities available across the Helios Electronics Segment. i3PD recently joined the Briggs & Stratton Vanguard™ Battery Technology Partner program , where it provides product design, engineering, and systems integration services for OEMs adopting Vanguard commercial battery technology. "We are thrilled to welcome i3 Product Development to our growing network of Vanguard Battery Technology Partners," said David Frank, Senior Vice President and President of Electrification at Briggs & Stratton. "By combining our proven battery technology with i3PD’s expertise in complex system integration, we can help OEMs confidently navigate the transition to electrified equipment." In addition, Enovation continues its supplier relationship with Ferris®, a Briggs & Stratton company, providing products including the PV485 display and IX3212 Power Distribution Module for commercial equipment applications. "These relationships demonstrate the diverse capabilities within our Electronics Segment," said Billy Aldridge, President, Electronics of Helios. "Whether through engineering services at i3PD or electronic control solutions from Enovation, our businesses create value for customers at different stages of product development and production. Together, they reflect the depth of expertise and customer-focused solutions we bring to the off-highway equipment market." About Briggs & Stratton Briggs & Stratton, headquartered in Milwaukee, Wisconsin, provides innovative products and diverse power solutions to help people get work done. Briggs & Stratton is the world’s largest producer of engines for lawn and garden, turf care and job site power equipment and is a leading designer, manufacturer and marketer of lithium-ion batteries, standby generators and energy storage systems through its Briggs & Stratton®, Vanguard®, Ferris®, Simplicity®, Snapper®, Billy Goat® and Branco® brands. Briggs & Stratton products are designed, manufactured, marketed and serviced in over 100 countries on six continents. Learn more at BriggsandStratton.com . About i3 Product Development i3 Product Development is a full-service product development firm that partners with leading manufacturers to design, engineer, and deliver innovative products. With expertise spanning mechanical and electrical engineering, industrial and UI/UX design, embedded systems, software development, and rapid prototyping, i3PD helps bring complex products to market with a focus on performance, reliability, and manufacturability. Learn more at i3pd.com and follow us on LinkedIn . About Enovation Controls Enovation Controls is a fast-growing and innovative manufacturer of electronic controls and displays for diverse markets. As an international leader in fully tailored solutions, Enovation Controls offers a broad range of displays, controls, and instrumentation products for various applications. With an internationally diverse team, we serve customers around the world through our global sales, manufacturing, and engineering operations. Enovation Controls partners directly with OEMs and supports a worldwide network of authorized distributors and system integrators. Visit us at www.enovationcontrols.com and follow us on LinkedIn . About Helios Technologies Helios Technologies is a global leader in highly engineered motion control and electronic controls technology, providing premium products that ensure safety, reliability, and seamless connectivity to diverse end markets including agriculture, construction, data centers, energy, health and wellness, industrial, marine, material handling, and recreational vehicles. Helios sells its products to customers in over 80 countries around the world. Its strategy is to be a diversified, customer-centric global enterprise distinguished by innovation, operational speed, and a high-performance culture. The Company has paid a cash dividend to its shareholders every quarter since becoming a public company in 1997. For more information please visit: www.heliostechnologies.com and follow us on LinkedIn . title: eCommerce email marketing: Strategies, types, and examples
summary: eCommerce email marketing drives sales, recovers carts, and builds loyalty. See the email types, campaign strategies, and examples that work across channels.
body_text: eCommerce email marketing is using email to promote products, recover lost sales, and build loyalty for an online store across the entire customer journey. It's one of the few channels you actually own. No social algorithm decides who sees your message, the list is yours, and it reliably returns more than it costs to run. This guide covers what eCommerce email marketing is, the email types worth sending, the strategies that lift revenue, how AI sharpens them, and real examples to borrow from. Throughout, you'll see why email performs best when you coordinate it with push, SMS, and in-app, and personalize it per shopper, rather than firing it off on its own. TL;DR eCommerce email marketing spans the full customer journey, from welcome and promotional campaigns to abandoned cart recovery, transactional messages, and post-purchase follow-ups. It's a direct, owned channel, so you reach customers without paying an algorithm for access, which makes retention-focused email some of the most cost-efficient revenue you have. A strong program mixes automated triggers, like welcome, cart recovery, and post-purchase, with scheduled campaigns, like promotions and seasonal sends. Email works hardest coordinated with push, SMS, and in-app under one customer profile, with frequency capping that keeps people from feeling swamped. AI adds two things: generative AI that creates content, subject lines, and image variations, and individual-level decisioning that picks the right message and send time for each customer. What is eCommerce email marketing? eCommerce email marketing is the practice of using email to drive sales, recover revenue, and build loyalty for an online store. It works across the customer journey, spanning acquisition, conversion, and retention. It blends automated triggered messages, like welcome, cart recovery, and post-purchase, with scheduled campaigns, like promotions and seasonal sends. Automated and scheduled emails An eCommerce email program runs on two types of send. Automated messages fire when a shopper takes an action, and scheduled campaigns go out on a calendar you set. Automated, or triggered, emails react to behavior in real time. A signup prompts a welcome email, an abandoned cart starts a recovery sequence, and a purchase fires a transactional email, then post-purchase follow-ups. These run on marketing automation, so they send without anyone hitting the button. Scheduled campaigns are the sends you plan and time yourself, like a product launch, a seasonal sale, or a monthly newsletter. You pick the audience and the moment. A direct channel you own Email is a direct line to your customers that no outside platform controls. You own the list, you decide what goes out, and your message reaches the inbox without an algorithm ranking it or charging you for reach. This separates email from rented channels like paid social and search ads, where visibility depends on a bidding system or a feed algorithm you don't control. The relationship sits between you and a subscriber who chose to hear from you, a steadier base to build repeat revenue on. Why email marketing matters for eCommerce Email matters for eCommerce because it's a direct channel you own, and it lifts results across acquisition, conversion, and retention. You aren't renting reach from a platform that can change its algorithm or its ad prices overnight. You're talking to people who asked to hear from you. Among retail and eCommerce , email is the favored engagement channel at 43%, ahead of messaging apps at 39% and SMS at 38%, according to the Retail Customer Engagement Review . It's also a channel brands keep funding, with global email marketing revenue reaching around $9.5 billion in 2024 and climbing since. Email marketing for online stores across the funnel Email works at all three stages of the shopping journey, covering acquisition, conversion, and retention through a single subscriber relationship. When email is in the mix, Braze research found shoppers are 89% more likely to purchase than those reached only on other channels, a real lift at the conversion stage rather than added awareness. Here's how the work splits across the funnel: Acquisition. A welcome series turns a new subscriber into a first-time buyer, often with an introductory offer to get the first purchase over the line. Conversion. Cart reminders, product recommendations, and well-timed promotions move hesitant shoppers toward checkout. Retention. Post-purchase follow-ups, loyalty rewards, and win-back sends bring existing customers back for the next order. Why retention makes email compound Retention is where email pays off hardest, because keeping a customer costs far less than winning a new one. The same shoppers show 81% longer average lifetimes when email is part of how they're reached. Since you own the channel, that added value arrives without the rising per-acquisition costs that paid channels carry, so returns accrue instead of resetting with every campaign. Handle retention this way and email becomes the engine of your lifecycle marketing, turning one-time buyers into a base of repeat revenue you can forecast. Types of eCommerce emails to send A complete eCommerce email marketing program leans on seven core types: welcome, transactional and post-purchase, abandoned cart, product recommendation, re-engagement and win-back, loyalty and rewards, and promotional and seasonal. Each is built for a different point in the customer's journey. Here's what each one does, when to send it, and what it's good for. Best for: Welcome series The first messages a new subscriber receives, sent right after they opt in. Engagement runs highest in those opening days, so a short welcome series is your best shot at turning fresh interest into a first order. Our roundup of the best welcome campaigns has examples worth stealing. Best for: Transactional and post-purchase emails A transactional email confirms an order, then shipping and delivery updates follow. People actively want these, so open rates run high, which makes them prime space for a loyalty nudge or a related-product suggestion once the essential info is covered. Best for: Abandoned cart emails Triggered when a shopper adds items but leaves before paying, usually as a short sequence rather than a single send. They're the highest-value trigger in eCommerce, because the shopper already showed intent. Our guide to abandoned cart recovery covers the timing, incentives, and flows in full. Best for: Product recommendation emails Personalized picks based on what a shopper browsed or bought, sent on a cadence or triggered by behavior. They work because relevance beats volume, a suggestion tied to real interest earns the click. Best for: Re-engagement and win-back emails Messages aimed at subscribers who've gone quiet, sent after a set stretch of inactivity. Reviving a lapsed customer costs far less than acquiring a new one, so even a modest recovery rate pays for itself. Best for: Loyalty and rewards emails Points updates, VIP perks, and birthday gifts sent to your loyalty segments or triggered by milestones. They make your best customers feel recognized, which nudges repeat purchases. Best for: Promotional and seasonal emails Scheduled sales, launches, and holiday campaigns timed to your calendar and to peak shopping moments. They drive volume and urgency, and they capitalize on high-intent windows like Black Friday and Cyber Monday. Examples of high-impact eCommerce email campaign strategies Here are eight high-impact eCommerce email campaign strategies that work to build relationships, relevance, and revenue: Personalized product recommendations. Use browse and purchase history to suggest what a shopper is likely to want next. Relevance drives the click, so you convert without leaning on a markdown. VIP and exclusive access. Give your best customers early access to launches and sales before anyone else. Exclusivity rewards loyalty and creates urgency without cutting the price. Back-in-stock and price-drop alerts. Tell shoppers when a sold-out item returns or a watched item gets cheaper. These reach people who already raised their hand, so intent runs high and conversion follows. First-purchase incentives. Give new subscribers a reason to place that first order, usually a small welcome discount or free shipping. This targets the one moment a discount actually pays for itself, turning a browser into a buyer. Win-back campaigns. Reach lapsed customers with a reminder of what they liked or a reason to come back. It costs far less than acquisition, and their history tells you exactly what to put in front of them. Referral and give-get. Reward existing customers for bringing friends, with both sides getting something. A recommendation from someone trusted converts better than any ad you could run. Milestone and anniversary. Mark a birthday or the anniversary of a first order with a note and maybe a perk. These land because they center on the customer rather than the sale. Social proof and UGC. Feature reviews, ratings, and real customer photos in your campaigns. Seeing genuine buyers reassures the hesitant ones and does the persuading for you. Why eCommerce email works best cross-channel The highest-performing eCommerce email programs coordinate with push, SMS, and in-app rather than running email in a silo. If you work from one unified customer profile, the channels reinforce each other. For example, you could have cart recovery messages sent across email and SMS , back-in-stock alerts via push, and promotions on the channel each customer responds to best, all sent at the time that suits that customer too. Run channels in silos and the shopper could receive all of those messages at once. With no frequency capping or consistency, the messages lose their relevance and create fatigue, no matter how good the content or the offer. Cross-channel orchestration solves that, with one profile, one coordinated cadence across everything you send. How AI improves eCommerce email marketing AI improves eCommerce email marketing in two distinct ways. Generative AI creates the content. AI decisioning works out what to send each customer and when. Generative AI for content and subject lines Generative AI drafts email copy, produces subject-line variants, and generates image variations far faster than a person building each from scratch. Feed it a brief and it returns several options to test, which keeps campaigns fresh as your subscriber base grows. It speeds up production of all your content, but you still edit, approve, and set the brand voice. AI decisioning for what to send and when AI decisioning handles the choices generative AI can't, picking the right message, offer, and moment for each individual person based on how they behave. It personalizes product recommendations, chooses the message most likely to drive the customer forward, and optimizes send time per person rather than blasting the whole list at 9 a.m. This individual-level decisioning is action optimization. BrazeAI Decisioning Studio™ does exactly this, making 1:1 decisions that optimize any business KPI you set, whether that's revenue, retention, or repeat purchase rate. Pair it with generative AI and you get relevant content delivered to the right person at the right moment, without a marketer hand-picking every send. How to build your eCommerce email marketing strategy (and measure it) To build an eCommerce email marketing strategy, follow these email marketing best practices . Pick a goal, work out who it's for, set your core sends to run on their own, then watch what comes back and adjust. The framework below runs in three stages, then covers the numbers that tell you it's working and the mistakes that stop most programs from growing. Stage 1: Set objectives and segment your audience Start with what you're trying to move and who you're talking to. Everything downstream depends on these two. Set clear objectives. Tie each campaign to a business outcome, more first orders, a higher repeat rate, fewer lapsed customers. The objective decides what you measure later. Segment your audience. Split your list by behavior, purchase history, and lifecycle stage so each message lands relevant. Strong segmentation runs on first-party data, the browsing, buying, and preference signals shoppers hand you directly. Stage 2: Use eCommerce email automation for your core sequences With goals and segments set, put automation to work. Build the triggered sequences that carry the most weight, then let them run on their own. Welcome series greets new subscribers while interest is highest. Cart recovery chases near-misses before intent fades. Post-purchase follows up with recent buyers. Win-back re-engages the ones going quiet. Marketing automation handles the timing on all four, so each fires the moment it's relevant instead of on your next send date. Stage 3: Sharpen and protect every send Good sequences still need sharp craft and a clean list behind them. This stage keeps your emails landing and your program healthy. Write subject lines and CTAs that earn the click. Keep subject lines short and specific, and give every email one clear call to action rather than three competing ones. Optimize for mobile. Most shoppers open on a phone, so single-column layouts, short copy, and tappable buttons aren't optional. Keep your list clean and compliant. Prune inactive subscribers to protect deliverability, use confirmed opt-ins, and follow the rules that apply to you, like GDPR and CAN-SPAM. Stage 4: Measure what matters Measure eCommerce email marketing success with a handful of metrics: open rate, click-through rate, conversion rate, revenue per email, unsubscribe rate, and bounce rate. Track these across every campaign and flow to see what's working and where value leaks: Metric What it tells you Open rate The share of recipients who open. Soft open rates usually point at the subject line or the sender name. Click-through rate (CTR) The share who click a link. Reads how well your content and CTA match what the subject line promised. Conversion rate The share who take the action you wanted, usually a purchase. The closest measure of business impact. Revenue per email Revenue generated divided by emails delivered. The truest read on what a single send is worth. Unsubscribe rate The share who opt out. A climbing rate signals fatigue or a mismatch with what people signed up for. Bounce rate The share that never reached an inbox. High bounces flag list-quality problems that drag down deliverability. Open rate. The share of recipients who open. Here's what each one looks like before it costs you: Emailing too much or too little. Over-send and people tune out or unsubscribe. Under-send and they forget you. Let engagement data set the cadence. Weak segmentation. Send the whole list one message and engagement drops while opt-outs climb. Flat subject lines. A dull subject line loses the open, and nothing downstream can win it back. Ignoring mobile. An email that breaks on a phone loses most of your audience before they read a word. Compliance missteps. Skipping consent or burying the unsubscribe link hurts deliverability and customer trust at once. body_text: Before the advent of mobile phones and the popularity of mobile FX trading platforms, dealers and brokers stood in loud, crowded rooms face-to-face, shouting prices and using hand signals to buy and sell currencies in trading pits. Then were the eras of telephone networks with dedicated phone lines, telex and fax machines, and physical money changers. But trading occurs around the clock, so traders have to keep track of the market even when going about their daily lives. That's where mobile FX trading apps come in handy. The best FX trading apps balance regulation, tight spreads, intuitive design, and educational resources. Top platforms in 2026 include MetaTrader 5, TradingView, IG, OANDA, and Interactive Brokers, each with its own strengths for different trader profiles. Beginners should prioritise apps with demo accounts, strong regulation, and clear risk warnings rather than the lowest spreads. FX trading apps let you trade currency pairs from your phone. The market is open 24 hours a day, five days a week, making mobile access more important than in most other asset classes. But the sheer number of apps available, ranging from serious professional platforms to barely regulated gambling-adjacent services, makes choosing carefully essential. This guide focuses on regulated, credible platforms. See our FX trading beginners’ guide if you are new to the space. Risk warning: Foreign exchange trading involves significant risk and is not suitable for all investors. You can lose more than your initial deposit. This article is for informational purposes only and does not constitute financial advice. Always verify that any platform you use is regulated in your jurisdiction before depositing funds. What to look for in a mobile FX trading platform Not every forex trading app is worth your money. Before opening an account, compare platforms based on the features that actually affect your trading experience and costs. Regulation Always choose a regulated broker. Regulation helps protect your funds and ensures the broker follows strict financial standards. UK: Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) US: Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) and National Futures Association (NFA) Australia: Australian Securities and Investments Commission (ASIC) If a broker isn't regulated by a recognised authority, it's best to avoid it. Spreads and commissions Every trade comes with a cost, usually in the form of spreads, commissions, or both. Don’t just take the advertised cost at face value. Some brokers advertise commission-free trading but make up for it with wider spreads. Others charge a commission while offering tighter spreads. Compare total trading costs rather than focusing on a single fee. Leverage FX platforms offer leverage, which can determine how much you stand to lose or gain in a trade. Leverage allows you to control a larger trading position with a smaller deposit, which also increases how much you risk losing. In the UK and EU, retail traders are limited to a maximum of 30:1 on major pairs under FCA/ESMA rules. In the US, CFTC limits retail leverage to 50:1 on major pairs. Higher leverage means higher risk. If you're new to forex, lower leverage is usually the safer choice. Demo account A demo account lets you practise with virtual money before risking real funds. You can learn how the platform works, test trading strategies, and understand how leverage affects your trades. If a platform does not offer a demo account, treat that as a warning sign. Mobile UX Since you'll be trading on your phone, the app should be fast, stable, and easy to navigate. Look for features such as: Real-time price charts Fast order execution Custom watchlists Price alerts Easy trade management Deposits and withdrawals Check how easy it is for you to fund your account and withdraw your money. Look out for fees that may apply. A good trading platform lets you know the deposit methods, withdrawal fees, processing times, and the minimum withdrawal amounts before you sign up. Check the platform’s reviews, and if they regularly mention delayed withdrawals, consider it a red flag. Works with dozens of regulated brokers, so you can choose pricing and leverage that fit your style. Cons Interface still feels denser than modern native apps. Charting and execution quality vary with the broker’s servers. Beginners can find the feature set overwhelming at first. 2. It does allow order execution through some connected brokers, but most traders use it for analysis and execute trades on a separate platform. Best for: Technical analysis, idea sharing and traders who want top-tier charts on mobile. Fees: Free plan available (limited); paid plans start at approximately $14.95 per month. Broker commissions/spreads apply when trading. Pros Best-in-class mobile charting with full Pine Script support and synced layouts across devices. Large community of shared ideas and scripts. Clean execution when linked to a compatible broker. Cons Not a broker itself. You still need a regulated trading account. Free version restricts indicators, alerts and multi-chart views. Cons Interface and account setup feel complex for pure beginners. Mobile experience prioritises depth over simplicity. Some advanced tools still work better on a desktop. 6. You can start from the easiest platform you can lay your hands on before moving to more complex articles. Start with a broker that offers: A free demo account Clear educational resources Transparent pricing Strong regulation An easy-to-use mobile app Practice with virtual money until you understand how orders work, what leverage means in practice, and how quickly losses can accumulate. Once you have had a good grasp of how the platform works, you can start committing real money. Platforms like Trading 212, XTB, and OANDA are designed for accessibility. They combine user-friendly interfaces with educational content and are regulated by the FCA for UK users. Be cautious with copy trading. Platforms like eToro allow you to automatically copy the trades of other users. This seems appealing, but it does not remove your risk. Copied traders can and do lose money. Avoid high leverage until you understand it. Even within regulatory limits, using maximum leverage as a beginner dramatically increases the chance of losing your entire deposit on a single trade going the wrong direction. How to evaluate FX trading app safety Before depositing any money, take a few minutes to verify that the broker is properly regulated. A legitimate broker should be easy to find on the relevant regulator's website. Check the regulator In the UK, search the broker on the Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) Register using its name or Firm Reference Number (FRN). In the US, use the NFA BASIC database to confirm the broker is registered with the Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) and is a member of the National Futures Association (NFA). If you can't find the broker on the appropriate register, don't open an account. Watch for these red flags Be cautious if a platform: Isn't listed on a recognised regulatory register Promises guaranteed profits or risk-free returns Pressures you to deposit more money quickly Makes withdrawals slow or unnecessarily difficult Advertises returns that seem far better than those of established, regulated brokers Understand what regulation protects Regulation helps protect your money if a broker becomes insolvent, but it doesn't protect you from trading losses. For example, eligible customers of firms that are authorised by the FCA may be entitled to the Financial Services Compensation Scheme (FSCS) for up to £85,000 if the broker collapses. However, this protection doesn't cover the money you lose on forex trades. FX trading apps vs currency exchange apps These are two different product categories, and it is worth being clear about the distinction. FX trading apps are speculative tools. You buy and sell currency pairs hoping to profit from price movements. You take on risk, you can lose money, and your gains (if any) come from correctly predicting price direction. Currency exchange apps like Grey are practical financial tools. You hold money in different currencies, convert when you need to, and use the funds for real purposes like paying invoices, receiving client income, or spending abroad. You are not speculating. You are managing money efficiently. If your goal is to speculate on exchange rates, you'll need a regulated forex broker. If your goal is to receive USD, EUR, or GBP payments from overseas clients, convert currencies, or send money internationally, a multi-currency account like Grey is a more suitable solution. Frequently asked questions What is the best FX trading app for beginners? Trading 212, XTB, and OANDA are consistently among the best for beginners right now. All three are FCA-regulated, offer demo accounts, have clean interfaces, and provide educational resources. Start with a demo account on any of them before trading with real money. Are FX trading apps safe? Regulated FX trading apps from FCA, CFTC, or ASIC-authorised brokers are legitimate financial products. The firms themselves are subject to regulatory oversight. However, the trading itself carries substantial risk: the FCA requires most UK FX brokers to publish figures showing what percentage of retail clients lose money, and for most brokers this figure is between 70% and 80%. Do FX trading apps work in the US? Yes, although US regulations limit the number of brokers that can serve retail traders. Well-known options include OANDA, FOREX.com , and Interactive Brokers. title: What Is TSMC? The Complete History of Morris Chang and the Foundry That Makes Everything (2026)
summary: TSMC history: Morris Chang, the 1987 pure-play foundry bet, yield as chipmaking's master metric, and why a single company makes about 90% of leading-edge logic.
body_text: Blog AI What Is TSMC? The Complete… On this page (18) Every conversation you have with an AI model, every frame a graphics card renders, every phone in every pocket — all of it runs on physical objects that somebody had to manufacture. The blog has already told the story of the company that designs the chips AI runs on and the story of the lab that trains the models . This is the story of the layer underneath both: the company that actually makes the silicon. TSMC does not design a single chip it sells. That is the entire point, and it was the strangest business idea in the semiconductor industry in 1987. This is how a man who failed his doctorate, chose a job over one dollar, and spent twenty-five years obsessed with a single manufacturing statistic ended up building the most consequential factory network on earth. 🧬 TL;DR: TSMC was founded in February 1987 on a promise no chip company had ever made: we will build your chips, and we will never design our own. That single non-compete guarantee created the fabless industry. TSMC is now worth roughly $2.16 trillion (23 July 2026) and makes about 90% of the world's leading-edge logic. See what AI builds on top of it → 🏭 What Is TSMC? Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company was incorporated on 21 February 1987 in Hsinchu, Taiwan, as the world's first pure-play foundry — a chip factory whose only business is manufacturing other companies' designs. By most estimates it now produces roughly 90% of the world's leading-edge logic (5nm and below) and about 70% of the total foundry market including mature nodes. Metric Value (as of 23 July 2026) Founded 21 February 1987, Hsinchu, Taiwan Founder Morris Chang (張忠謀), aged 55 at founding Business model Pure-play foundry — manufactures only, designs nothing Market capitalization ~$2.16 trillion — 6th most valuable company in the world Leading-edge logic share ~90% at 5nm and below (by most estimates) Total foundry market share ~70% including mature nodes US expansion Six-fab complex in Arizona; $6.6B CHIPS Act support against a $165B+ company commitment Two of those numbers deserve care. The market cap is a dated figure — TSMC crossed $2 trillion on 25 February 2026 and rose roughly 93% over the preceding twelve months, so any TSMC valuation quoted without a date is probably already wrong. And the 90% figure applies specifically to leading-edge logic ; the car in your driveway is full of mature-node silicon from dozens of other fabs. What makes TSMC unusual is not scale. It is the shape of the business. Before 1987, if you wanted to sell a chip, you had to own a factory. TSMC broke that requirement and brought an entire industry into existence. 🔀 What Is a Pure-Play Foundry, and Why Didn't It Exist Before 1987? A pure-play foundry manufactures designs owned by other companies and owns none of its own. Integrated device manufacturers — Intel, Texas Instruments, NEC — had sold spare capacity for years, but they also sold competing chips, so handing over a design meant arming a rival. TSMC's innovation was contractual, not technical : it promised never to compete with its customers. Read that diagram left to right and you are looking at the most consequential interface in modern computing. On the left, a designer with an idea and no factory. On the right, a factory with no ideas of its own. The arrow between them is worth trillions of dollars, and it did not exist until a 55-year-old executive who had just been passed over for promotion drew it. One precision point: TSMC did not invent the foundry. It invented the pure-play foundry — and Chang had already pitched the idea inside Texas Instruments in 1976 and been turned down. He carried a rejected proposal for eleven years before he found a company to build it with. 🌏 Who Is Morris Chang? Morris Chang was born on 10 July 1931 in Ningbo, Zhejiang — not Taiwan, a place he would not visit until 1968 and not live in until 1985. By the age of eighteen he had fled war three times, lived in six cities, and changed schools ten times . That accounting is his own, not a biographer's. The sequence reads like a map of a collapsing century. Guangzhou, where his father was a bank manager. British Hong Kong, after Japan bombed the city in 1937. Japanese-occupied Shanghai. Then, in late March 1943, a fifty-day crossing of the front lines into "Free China," ending at Chongqing and a place at the selective Nankai Middle School. He wanted to be a writer. His father's verdict, as Chang reproduces it in his memoir: 「會餓肚子的」— "You'll go hungry." In July 1949 , days after his eighteenth birthday, he flew Pan Am out of Hong Kong's Kai Tak airport to San Francisco. He wrote in his diary aboard the plane: "Lifting into the sky, I looked back with a heavy heart; Hong Kong was already lost in the clouds… crossing an ocean to a country I did not know, the road ahead utterly obscure — how could I not feel sorrow?" One year at Harvard — the only Chinese student in his class — then a transfer to MIT for mechanical engineering (BS 1952, MS 1953). His stated reason for transferring was job prospects. Then the door closed. 🚪 Why Did Morris Chang Call Failing His Doctorate "The Greatest Stroke of Luck in My Life"? Chang failed the MIT doctoral qualifying exam twice . He described the moment as "the greatest blow of my life. My self-esteem and self-confidence were destroyed in an instant." Decades later, having built TSMC, he called the same failure "the greatest stroke of luck in my life" — because a doctorate would have routed him into academia and away from semiconductors entirely. It is worth being careful with that second quote. It is a founder narrating an accident in hindsight, which is a genre with a known bias. What it does establish is the shape of the life: the closed door pushed him into industry, and industry pushed him into a factory, and the factory is where he found the idea he would spend forty years on. The rejection had one immediate consequence. Instead of a doctorate, he needed a job. 💵 How Did One Dollar Send Morris Chang Into Semiconductors? Chang had four job offers and was leaning toward Ford — stable, prestigious, the safe choice. Ford offered $479 a month . Sylvania offered $480 . He phoned Ford to ask about the difference and was told: "We do not haggle. The company has decided on your salary. If you want to join, come. If not, then farewell." He chose Sylvania over one dollar and a tone of voice. That decision put a mechanical engineer inside a brand-new transistor lab , where he had to teach himself device physics from William Shockley's 1950 textbook , Electrons and Holes in Semiconductors . His method was unglamorous and effective: he brought the book to the bar after work and bought drinks for senior colleagues so they would answer his questions about it. He also carried one sentence out of Sylvania, from the semiconductor division's general manager, that he says he organized a career around: "Our trouble at Sylvania is that we cannot make what we can sell and we cannot sell what we can make." Sylvania was betting on germanium. A small company in Dallas was mass-producing silicon . In 1958, Chang joined it. 📉 What Is Yield, and Why Is It the Master Metric of Chipmaking? Yield is the share of dies on a wafer that come out working . It is driven by defect density and falls exponentially as die size grows , because a bigger die is a bigger target for the same random contamination. Yield is the number the whole business turns on: a wafer costs the same to process whether its dies pass or fail, so raising yield collapses cost per good chip without adding a single machine. Texas Instruments handed the 24-year-veteran-to-be that exact problem on his arrival in 1958. He took a near-zero line to roughly 20–30% , and built a reputation as someone who understood manufacturing at the level of physics rather than management. TI thought highly enough of him to pay full salary and tuition to send him to Stanford ; he came back two and a half years later with a PhD in electrical engineering (1964) . The arithmetic he was fighting is unforgiving. The simplest textbook model treats defects as randomly scattered across the wafer, which gives yield as Y = e^(-D₀ × A) — where D₀ is defects per square centimetre and A is die area: Die area Yield at D₀ = 0.1 /cm² What this means 10 mm² (small controller) ~99% Almost everything works 50 mm² ~95% Still comfortable 100 mm² (1 cm²) ~90% Every tenth die is scrap 400 mm² ~67% A third of the wafer is thrown away 800 mm² (large AI die) ~45% More than half the wafer is scrap Those are illustrative numbers from a standard model, not TSMC's internal figures — but the shape is real, and it is why the biggest chips in the world are the hardest ones to make money on. Double the die and you do not lose twice as much. You lose exponentially more. 🇯🇵 What Did the 1981 Miho Discovery Reveal? In 1981 , Texas Instruments found that its Miho fab in Japan was running memory yields of 40–50% — roughly double the yields at its Houston fab. Chang was sent to find out why. What he found was not a machine. It was ~2% employee turnover in Japan against 10–25% in Houston , and technically educated shift leaders and equipment engineers standing on the line. In the Japanese fab, the people who knew how the equipment behaved on a bad night were still there the following year, and the year after that. In Houston they were not, because top American engineering graduates would not take factory-floor jobs at all. (Chang's own retelling adds that the leading candidate for one US supervisor slot held a degree in French literature; that detail comes from him and is not independently verified.) Yield, it turned out, was not primarily a physics problem. It was an institutional memory problem. The conclusion Chang drew was blunt: the future of advanced manufacturing was not in the United States. Six years later, he would act on it. 🚶 Why Did Morris Chang Leave Texas Instruments at 51? By the late 1970s, Texas Instruments was pivoting toward calculators and digital watches, and the man who had spent his career on manufacturing physics was watching the company move away from him. After 25 years , at 51 , with no realistic path to chief executive, Chang resigned with nothing lined up. He became president and chief operating officer of General Instrument in New York. The work was acquisitions, and it bored him. What mattered in that stretch was a single conversation. Gordon Campbell — later a co-founder of Chips and Technologies, one of the first fabless semiconductor companies — approached Chang while trying to raise $50 million for a chip company. Campbell came back some time later and said he now needed only a fraction of that, because he had subcontracted the fabrication instead of building a fab. That was the proof. Design and manufacturing had quietly become two different businesses, and only one of them required a billion-dollar plant. Chang had proposed exactly this arrangement at TI in 1976 and been refused. Now somebody had done it accidentally, and the numbers worked. 🏗️ How Did TSMC Actually Get Founded in 1987? K.T. Li — conventionally called the godfather of Taiwan's technology industry — recruited Chang to head ITRI in 1985 and told him the government wanted Taiwan to have a semiconductor company. It was effectively a blank cheque with no product attached. The pure-play foundry was Chang's answer to that brief, devised afterwards — not a plan he was hired to execute. In February 1987 TSMC was incorporated on a promise no chip company had ever made: We will build your chips, and we will never design our own. The bet was contractual rather than technical. A fabless startup could hand over its crown-jewel design without arming a competitor, because the factory had no products of its own to defend. That single guarantee of neutrality is what made the fabless industry possible: thousands of designers who could never have afforded a fab, and one foundry whose scale came from serving all of them at once. It did not look inevitable. Intel refused to invest. Then in late 1987 , roughly nine months after incorporation, Andy Grove turned up to inspect the fab. Intel ran TSMC through its qualification process. TSMC passed, and Intel became its first American customer , ordering legacy 1.5-micron parts. It is worth killing a myth here. The story is often told as Chang setting out to take on the giants of the day. He did not. The foil was never a company — it was the integrated model itself, the arrangement in which one firm both designs and manufactures. Intel became a customer, not a target. And the Korean chip industry that would eventually enter foundry work was not a factor in 1987 at all; that competition arrives roughly thirty years later. ✉️ How Did TSMC and NVIDIA Find Each Other? In 1997 , NVIDIA was down to about 60 people and nearly out of money. Jensen Huang had got nowhere with TSMC's San Jose sales office, so he mailed a letter . It reached Morris Chang, who telephoned him unannounced. The deal was signed in 1998 , and it has compounded for nearly thirty years. One correction, because it is the single most-repeated error about this relationship: the RIVA 128 was not a TSMC chip. It was built by SGS-Thomson on a 350nm process and shipped on 25 August 1997 — before the letter produced a contract. NVIDIA's first TSMC part was the RIVA TNT , launched on 31 August 1998 . The video-essay version of this story routinely credits TSMC with both, and the timeline refutes it on its own terms. For Chang's 2018 retirement, Huang commissioned an artist-rendered comic timeline of their friendship, which hangs in Chang's Taipei office. In the accompanying letter, read at the retirement dinner, Huang wrote that Chang's career was "a masterpiece, like Beethoven's Ninth Symphony." 👔 Who Actually Ran TSMC, and When? Chang was chairman from the founding in 1987 , not chief executive. Philips, an early investor, supplied TSMC's first CEO, James E. Dykes . Chang's own CEO tenure came later and in two separate stints, separated by four years. Period Morris Chang's role Feb 1987 → 1998 Chairman (Philips supplied the first CEO, James E. Dykes) Mar 1998 → Jun 2005 Chairman and CEO Jun 2005 → Jun 2009 Chairman Jun 2009 → 12 Nov 2013 Chairman and CEO (second stint) Nov 2013 → 5 Jun 2018 Chairman; CEO duties to co-CEOs Mark Liu and C.C. Wei The "founder-CEO for eighteen straight years" version of this story is wrong in both directions: it gives him a title he did not hold in 1987 and merges two separate stints into one run. Chang retired on 5 June 2018 , thirty-one years after incorporation. 📏 Do "3nm" and "2nm" Mean Anything Physical? No. They are marketing names for process generations , not measurements. Nothing on a 3nm chip is 3nm across. Transistor pitch on an N3-class process is closer to 48nm — roughly 1,500 times finer than a human hair, which is impressive without needing to be exaggerated. The features that genuinely measure a handful of nanometres are specific structures: nanosheet channel thicknesses and fin widths in the 5–10nm range, which really are thousands of times thinner than a hair. But the node number on the marketing sheet is a generation label, not a ruler reading, and has been for over a decade. Treat "3nm" the way you treat a car model year. Being pedantic here matters for the same reason yield matters: the marketing number and the engineering number diverged, and the industry kept using both. The AI industry is currently repeating the pattern. 📊 Why Does the AI Industry Measure Capability but Almost Never Measure Yield? Chang made yield the master metric of an entire industry — the one number the factory is organized around. The AI industry measures capability relentlessly, through benchmarks, leaderboards and evaluation suites, and measures yield almost never. But the yield numbers are everywhere once you know the unit to look for. Each of the results below was reported publicly by the team that produced it, and none of them were framed as yield: Publicly reported result Yield reading AlphaProof solved 9 of 353 Erdős problems 2.5% good die per wafer An engineering team's agent PR-success ramp, ~20–30% → ~80% A textbook yield ramp on a production line An overnight research loop producing 20 genuine improvements from 700 experiments 2.9% — and the 680 failures still cost compute An agentic review pipeline catching a mistake in 63% of ~1,000 changes across 59 repos A defect-detection rate, measured like final test Every one of those is stated in Chang's units — good units out of units started — and almost none of them are reported that way. We unpack that unit in full in what yield means for AI systems . And the moment you accept the unit, the arithmetic that governs a fab starts governing agent runs too, because yields multiply along a chain : SERIAL YIELD: Y = y₁ × y₂ × y₃ × … × yₙ A 30-step agent run: 99.0% per step → 0.99³⁰ = 74% "excellent benchmark, one in four runs fails" 95.0% per step → 0.95³⁰ = 21% "good benchmark, four in five runs fail" 90.0% per step → 0.90³⁰ = 4% "respectable benchmark, effectively unusable" The per-step number barely moved. The end-to-end number collapsed. This is the quantitative reason long-horizon agent autonomy degrades in a way per-step benchmarks never show . A model that is 95% reliable on any individual action sounds close to solved. Chain thirty of those actions and four runs in five contain at least one error. Our writeup on how AI agents actually stay reliable covers the complementary half of the algebra — independent checkers, where miss rates multiply in your favour instead of against you. Chang's doctrine points at the fix, and it is not more inspection. A fab buys yield by raising each individual step and encoding quality into the process — in software terms, agent evaluations at the step level, guardrails that fire before a bad state propagates, deterministic gates rather than a vibe check at the end, and a harness that can retry one step instead of a whole run. It is also why AI-generated apps break the way they do: the failure was manufactured thirty steps ago and only observed at final test. One more Chang lesson is buried in that table. Final test must be independent of the thing being tested. A wafer probe is a separate machine with its own calibration. When the model that wrote the code also certifies the code, you have a probe wired to the stepper — a failure mode production agent deployments hit constantly. 🧬 What Does the Foundry Trade Look Like in Software? The foundry trade is a clean division of labour: the customer brings domain intent, and the factory brings manufacture. Taskade Genesis makes structurally the same trade — you describe the app you need in a prompt, and the platform assembles the working version, with the projects, agents and automations wired up behind it. That trade is why a foundry matters. A chip designer in 1990 could ship a product without ever touching a stepper. A clinic owner or a field-services operator in 2026 can ship a working internal tool without ever touching a deployment pipeline. In both cases, somebody with deep domain knowledge and no manufacturing capability got access to a factory. The foundry trade Taskade Genesis equivalent Customer supplies the design intent You supply the prompt and the domain knowledge Foundry supplies the process node The platform supplies generation, hosting, custom domains and SSL Customer never touches a stepper You never touch a build pipeline — see your first app Test and binning before shipment Version history and error fixing before you publish Packaged parts ship to market Publishing an app to your own domain or the Community Gallery One honest caveat, because the analogy has a limit. TSMC's founding promise was neutrality — we will never compete with our customers. Taskade does not make that promise and should not pretend to. Taskade ships first-party starter kits, and published apps are surfaced in the Community Gallery where other people can clone them. That may well be the better business — the next builder skips the blank prompt entirely — but it is a different arrangement from the one Chang made in 1987. The yield idea transfers exactly, though. On the execution side, Taskade already reports something Chang would recognize: automations carry a health signal computed from recent run history , and every run keeps a step-by-step log with per-step inputs and outputs. That is process control, not a satisfaction survey — it tells you which step is dragging the line down. Extending that discipline from automations to everything an AI agent manufactures is where the whole industry is heading, whether it calls the number "yield" or not. Memory feeds Intelligence, Intelligence triggers Execution, Execution creates Memory — the Workspace DNA loop is a production line, and production lines have yields. Build your first app free → 🕰️ Morris Chang and TSMC: The Timeline Morris Chang's career spans sixty years , from a near-zero yield line at Texas Instruments in 1958 to a $2.16 trillion company he retired from in June 2018. The dates below are the load-bearing ones, and several of them contradict the version of this story that circulates online. Year Event 1931 Born 10 July in Ningbo, Zhejiang 1937–1943 Guangzhou → Hong Kong → occupied Shanghai → 50-day crossing to Chongqing 1949 Flies Pan Am from Kai Tak to San Francisco; Harvard freshman year 1952–1953 MIT — BS then MS in mechanical engineering ~1955 Fails the MIT doctoral qualifier twice; chooses Sylvania over Ford by one dollar 1958 Joins Texas Instruments; assigned the yield problem 1964 PhD in electrical engineering, Stanford — funded by TI 1976 Pitches a foundry model inside TI; rejected 1981 Miho fab in Japan runs 40–50% memory yield, roughly double Houston's ~1983 Leaves TI at 51 after 25 years; president and COO at General Instrument 1985 Recruited by K.T. Li to head ITRI in Taiwan 1987 TSMC incorporated 21 February; Andy Grove visits in late 1987; Intel becomes first American customer 1997–1998 Jensen Huang's letter; deal signed 1998; RIVA TNT is the first TSMC NVIDIA part 1998–2005 Chairman and CEO 2009–2013 Chairman and CEO, second stint 2018 Retires as chairman on 5 June 2026 ~$2.16 trillion market cap; 6th most valuable company in the world (23 July) 🤔 What Is the Lesson of Morris Chang's Career? The lesson is that an interface can be worth more than an invention . Chang did not invent the transistor, the wafer, or lithography. He drew a line between two activities that had always been done by the same company, and let a different firm stand on each side of it. That is a repeatable move, and it keeps happening. Hosting accounts separated running a website from owning a server. Cloud computing separated running software from owning a data center. Open-weight models separated owning a model's design from being able to manufacture its inference — publishing the blueprint changes who owns it and nothing about who can run it. It comes with a warning too: the layer that creates the value does not automatically capture it. Telecom carriers moved orders of magnitude more data over twenty-five years and their equities went nowhere. TSMC captured the profits of its split. Most infrastructure does not. "We are the foundry of X" has to be earned in margin, not asserted in a keynote. The second lesson is quieter and more useful. Chang won by caring about a number nobody else found interesting. Everybody in 1958 wanted to talk about what a transistor could do. He spent forty years on what fraction of them worked. The capability question is the fun one, and the industry is full of people asking it. The yield question is the one that decides whether a factory — of chips, of software, of agent runs — is a business or a demonstration. 🐑 Before you go ... title: How To Build a Successful Nurse Residency Program in 2026
summary: Learn how to build a successful nurse residency program, from curriculum design and competency tracking to ANCC PTAP accreditation readiness and nurse retention strategies.
body_text: KEY TAKEAWAYS: Build a structured nurse residency program with a clear curriculum. ​Validate clinical competency through assessments and checklists. ​​Use simulation to strengthen clinical decision-making. ​Develop communication, resilience, and emotional intelligence skills. ​Support new nurses through mentorship and preceptor guidance. ​Measure success through retention, competency, and engagement metrics Align the program with American Nurses Credentialing Center Practice Transition Accreditation Program (ANCC PTAP) accreditation standards. How nurse residency programs strengthen clinical readiness ‍ New graduate nurses face one of the steepest learning curves in any profession. They leave academic programs with strong foundational knowledge, but the realities of clinical practice require a different level of readiness — one that develops through time, support, and hands-on experience. A well-designed nurse residency program supports this growth. ​For healthcare organizations, the stakes couldn't be higher. Nurse turnover is expensive, patient safety depends on clinical confidence, and the nursing workforce itself is under sustained pressure. Nurse residency programs have emerged as one of the most effective ways to address all three challenges at once. ​This guide explains what a strong nurse residency program looks like in 2026, from curriculum design and competency development to accreditation readiness and long-term measurement. What is a nurse residency program? ​A nurse residency program is a structured, employer-based transition to practice program designed to support new graduate nurses as they move from academic education into clinical practice. Most programs run between 12 and 24 months, with 12 months being the standard recommended by the American Association of Colleges of Nursing (AACN) . ​The primary goals are to build clinical competence, reduce new-nurse turnover, and support patient safety. Rather than leaving new nurses to navigate unfamiliar environments on their own, residency programs provide a structured pathway with mentorship, skill development, and regular feedback built in from day one. Most programs run between 12 and 24 months, with 12 months being the standard recommended by the American Association of Colleges of Nursing (AACN). ​Why nurse residency programs matter more than ever in 2026 ​The nursing workforce is under pressure from multiple directions. Retaining experienced nurses, preparing new graduates, and maintaining safe staffing levels are all challenges that intersect directly with how well organizations support early-career nurses. Nurse residency programs address each of these challenges in meaningful ways. ​Addressing nurse turnover ​First-year nurse turnover remains one of the most costly workforce challenges in healthcare. According to NSI Nursing Solutions , the average cost of turnover for a bedside registered nurse now exceeds $60,000. However, nurse residency programs are consistently associated with lower first-year attrition, giving organizations a concrete way to protect their workforce investment. ​The average cost of turnover for a bedside RN now exceeds $60,000, but nurse residency programs are associated with lower first-year turnover. ​Building clinical confidence ​New graduates often report feeling underprepared for the realities of clinical practice. A structured transition to practice program addresses this directly by pairing progressive learning plans with hands-on experience, simulation, and regular competency assessments. ​Supporting patient safety ​Clinical errors are more likely when nurses feel uncertain or lack sufficient support. Research from the National Council of State Boards of Nursing (NCSBN) has linked structured transition-to-practice programs to improved patient safety outcomes, making residency programs a quality-of-care issue, not just a workforce one. ​Preparing the future nursing workforce ​The nursing profession is facing a generational shift. As experienced nurses retire, organizations need a reliable pipeline of prepared, confident clinicians. Nurse residency programs build that pipeline in a structured, consistent way rather than leaving new-nurse readiness to chance. ​The essential components of a successful nurse residency program ​Structured residency curriculum ​A strong nurse residency curriculum goes beyond orientation checklists. It includes core clinical topics applicable to all new nurses, specialty learning tracks for units like ICU, emergency, or perioperative care, and progressive learning plans that build complexity over time. The goal is a logical progression in which each stage builds the skills and confidence nurses need for the next. ​Competency development ​Clinical competency validation is the backbone of any effective nurse residency program. Skills assessments and competency checklists give educators and leaders a clear picture of where each nurse stands, and where additional support is needed. HealthStream's Competency Suite supports this process by enabling organizations to standardize competency tracking, manage checklists, and maintain documentation in one place — making it easier to identify gaps before they affect patient care. ​Simulation and scenario-based learning ​Realistic patient scenarios allow new nurses to practice critical thinking and clinical decision-making in a safe environment. Simulation gives learners a safe space to make mistakes, reflect on their decisions, and improve — without risk to patients. Organizations that invest in scenario-based learning report stronger clinical confidence among residency graduates. ​Communication and emotional intelligence ​Technical skills alone don't determine a nurse's effectiveness. Team communication, conflict resolution, patient communication, resilience, and self-awareness all shape how new nurses perform under pressure. A well-rounded nurse residency program incorporates these skills deliberately, rather than assuming they'll develop on their own. ​Mentorship and preceptor support ​Preceptors are among the most important resources a new nurse has. Structured preceptor training, clear coaching frameworks, and regular feedback loops give preceptors the tools they need to support residents effectively. Peer support structures also matter, as new nurses benefit from connecting with others navigating similar challenges. ​Measuring nurse residency program success ​Measuring program outcomes is essential to evaluating and improving a nurse residency program. The following indicators give organizations a reliable picture of program effectiveness. ​Nurse confidence surveys ​Regular confidence surveys track how new nurses feel about their clinical readiness over time. Trends across cohorts can reveal gaps in the curriculum or areas where simulation or mentorship could be strengthened. ​Retention rates ​First-year and second-year retention rates are among the clearest indicators of program impact. Organizations should track retention by unit, specialty, and cohort to identify patterns. ​Competency achievement ​Tracking the percentage of residents who meet competency benchmarks on schedule, and those who require remediation, helps educators refine learning plans and allocate support resources appropriately. ​ ​Engagement metrics ​Participation rates, assessment completion, and learning activity engagement all signal how invested residents are in the program. Low engagement often points to content, scheduling, or support issues worth addressing. ​Program dashboards and reporting ​Centralizing program data in a reporting dashboard makes it easier for nurse leaders to see the full picture and make informed decisions. HealthStream's Competency Suite supports this with reporting tools that consolidate competency data, assessment results, and completion rates across departments and specialties. ​ Preparing for ANCC PTAP and Magnet recognition ​The ANCC Practice Transition Accreditation Program provides a formal framework for evaluating and recognizing transition to practice programs. Achieving PTAP accreditation signals a meaningful commitment to new-nurse development and is closely linked to Magnet recognition. ​Accreditation readiness requires consistent documentation, organized evidence collection, and a culture of continuous improvement. Organizations that use structured tools to manage competency records and program data are better positioned to meet these requirements without scrambling to compile evidence at audit time. ​Common challenges when building a nurse residency program ​Even well-resourced organizations run into predictable obstacles: ​Limited educator resources: Nursing professional development practitioners are stretched thin. Programs that rely too heavily on a single educator or department are vulnerable to gaps. ​Inconsistent curriculum: Without standardization, program quality varies across units, shifts, and cohorts. ‍ ​Tracking competency across specialties: Managing competency data for nurses in different units often means having to work across disconnected systems. ‍ ​Measuring outcomes: Many organizations track completion rates while failing to measure other critical measures, including clinical confidence, retention, or patient outcomes. ‍ Administrative burden: Documentation and reporting requirements can consume significant time if not supported by the right tools. ​Recognizing these challenges early makes it easier to build a program designed to address them from the start. ​Best practices for launching or improving your program ​Use this checklist as a practical starting point for building or strengthening a nurse residency program: ​ Step 1: Establish clear, measurable learning objectives for each program phase ‍ Step 2: Standardize the curriculum across units and specialties ‍ Step 3: Incorporate simulation and scenario-based learning into the core program ‍ Step 4: Measure both confidence and clinical competency at regular intervals ‍ Step 5: Use data to identify gaps and continuously improve outcomes ‍ Step 6: Build structured mentorship opportunities with trained preceptors ‍ Step 7: Align program design and documentation with ANCC PTAP standards ‍ Step 8: Evaluate program performance at the end of each cohort and adjust accordingly ​ ​FAQs ​How long should a nurse residency program last? ‍ Most accreditation bodies, including the ANCC and AACN, recommend a minimum of 12 months. Some specialty areas, such as critical care or perioperative nursing, may benefit from longer programs of up to 24 months. ​What should be included in a nurse residency curriculum? ‍ A complete nurse residency curriculum includes core clinical content, specialty learning tracks, simulation-based learning, communication and emotional intelligence development, competency assessments, and structured mentorship. ​How do nurse residency programs improve retention? By building clinical confidence and providing structured support during the most vulnerable period of a nurse's career, nurse residency programs reduce the isolation and uncertainty that often drive early turnover. ​What is ANCC PTAP? The ANCC PTAP is a formal accreditation pathway that recognizes healthcare organizations for the quality of their transition to practice programs. It provides a structured framework for program design, documentation, and continuous improvement. ​ How do you measure the success of a nurse residency program? ‍ Key metrics include nurse confidence survey results, first-year and second-year retention rates, competency achievement rates, engagement with program activities, and overall program completion. Reporting dashboards help consolidate these data points for ongoing review. ​What is the difference between nurse orientation and a residency program? Nurse orientation is typically a brief, compliance-focused introduction to an organization's policies and procedures. A nurse residency program is a longer, structured developmental experience that builds clinical competence, professional identity, and long-term readiness for practice.

title: The Mayflower Update
summary: A new dawn for Bean Farmers.
body_text: On Season 6074, as the early dawn light broke across the rolling fields, the Farmers of Beanstalk gathered on the Mayflower, their trusty vessel, ready to set sail towards a new horizon. They had weathered many storms and worked hard to tend to their recovered crops, but they knew that in order to grow and thrive, they needed to adapt and evolve. Today, Beanstalk Farms is excited to announce the Mayflower Update and an anticipated launch timeline. Note: BIP-34 Sunrise Improvements and BIP-35: Stalk Delegation and Process Amendments were proposed today! The Mayflower Update consists of three major changes that will significantly improve the way the Beanstalk community experiences farming: (1) Sunrise Improvements, (2) Silo V3 and (3) Basin. Sunrise Improvements Today, the Sunrise Improvements BIP is live for voting . The Sunrise Improvements upgrade is primarily composed of 2 changes: Morning Auction When the Bean price is above peg, Beanstalk still issues Soil in order to measure demand for Soil (and consequently adjust the Temperature). However, during times of short-term excess demand for Soil, Beanstalk pays significantly more in Pods than is necessary to attract creditors. During the Morning of each Season (the first 5 minutes, or 25 blocks), the Temperature offered by Beanstalk is dynamic. Each Morning, the offered Temperature ramps from 1% to 100% of the maximum Temperature. The Morning Auction should reduce unnecessary Pod issuance, which should improve Beanstalk’s creditworthiness as a borrower. In addition, maximizing Beans borrowed for a given Pod issuance improves Beanstalk’s efficiency. Here's a preview of the new Field page in the Beanstalk UI: Sunrise Incentive Adjustment Beanstalk updates its monetary policy every Season, which occurs upon a successful call of the sunrise function. It costs gas to call the sunrise function and Beanstalk often overpays in Beans to incentivize users to call it. The Sunrise Incentive Adjustment upgrade makes it such that how much Beanstalk pays for incentivization of the sunrise function takes into account Ethereum network conditions (i.e., current gas costs) and Beanstalk economic conditions (i.e., the Bean price). Reducing unnecessary Bean issuance in the sunrise incentive reward should reduce sell pressure on Beans. Silo V3 The Silo V3 upgrade introduces multiple composability and UX improvements to the Silo, one of the core components of Beanstalk. Removal of the Withdrawal Timer When Beanstalk was launched in August 2021, Farmers had to wait 24 Seasons before being able to claim Withdrawn assets from the Silo. This lockup period likely served Beanstalk well during its infancy stage. Now that Beanstalk is more established, and more participants understand the incentives of the Stalk System, it has become clear that the Withdrawal timer is an economic inefficiency that creates a supply overhang when there are Withdrawn assets. Since Replant, the Withdrawal timer has lasted until the remainder of the current Season. Now that the Withdrawal timer is being removed, Bean seigniorage will be distributed based on a time-weighted average, rather than based Stalk at the end of the Season. Distributing seigniorage this way eliminates the profit of a potential attack where a user deposits assets in the Silo, calls sunrise , earns Bean seigniorage and withdraws the assets all in a single transaction while retaining Bean exposure for zero blocks. Examples of developments that become possible after the removal of the Withdrawal timer include the redemption of Roots for Circulating Beans in a single transaction, the ability to order Pods on the Market with Deposits, etc. Tokenization of Deposits as ERC-1155s Making the positive carry of holding Beans usable in DeFi is critical to the success of Beanstalk. In practice, this means facilitating economic activity in Silo Deposits, given that it is Deposits that earn Bean inflation (and not Beans that are held outside the Silo). To that end, tokenizing Deposits and having them conform to an established ERC standard like ERC-1155 is a necessary step in this direction. This will immediately provide utility in the form of a permissionless market for Deposits on existing infrastructure like OpenSea. Dynamic Seeds per BDV Currently, there is no straightforward way to change the Seeds per BDV rewards for a given Silo Deposit type. After Silo V3, it will be possible for the DAO to adjust the Seeds reward for a given whistlisted asset via BIP. This serves as the technical foundation for a future Gauge System where the DAO can express preferences that lead to Stalk and Seed rewards for various whitelisted assets changing in real time. Unripe Seeds Parity Currently, Unripe Bean Deposits receive 2 Seeds per BDV and Unripe BEAN:3CRV LP Deposits receive 4 Seeds per BDV. Most Bean liquidity is underlying Unripe LP, but converting to Unripe Beans results in a loss of Seeds. This seems to be one of the primary reasons for why a significant amount of Unripe LP remains in the Silo despite the opportunity to convert to Unripe Beans to arbitrage the Bean price. Changing the Seed rewards for both Unripe assets to the same value would remove a significant cost to converting from Unripe LP to Unripe Beans. This may result in more conversions, which would have a significant effect on peg maintenance. A DAO vote is likely in order to determine what the exact Seeds per BDV values for Unripe Beans and Unripe BEAN:3CRV LP should be set to in Silo V3. Basin Liquidity pools on the upcoming DEX are known as Wells, but the overall DEX architecture is known as Basin. Give the new Basin Twitter account a follow. There are a number of problems with current implementations of AMMs on Ethereum. In a post-Merge environment, existing on-chain AMMs are not multi-block MEV resistant. Given that Beanstalk needs to price Beans against other assets (on-chain) and that the goal of Beanstalk is to be as censorship and manipulation resistant as possible, multi-block MEV is an attack vector that should be addressed. Additionally, most AMMs in DeFi are generally not designed to be composable and have little flexibility in allowing developers customize their liquidity pool implementation. Trading fees, pricing functions, and price oracles are embedded and cannot be customized independently. Basin aims to solve these problems: Pumps, the oracles of the Basin DEX are composable and customizable by design. The first implementation developed by Beanstalk Farms provides the first multi-block MEV resistant oracle implementation on the Ethereum network. Developers can utilize the work of other ecosystem contributors and the Beanstalk DAO who develop, audit and deploy custom pricing functions, Pump implementations, and even new pool factory contracts. The composability of Basin also allows for the deployment of Wells with zero trading fees. Providing liquidity to Wells which do not collect trading fees can be incentivized via protocol-native incentives, such as whitelisting the Well LP token in the Silo. See Publius' Worthless Tech and Beanstalk Development Update writeups for a deep-dive. Basin Integration Launching Basin in a way that Beanstalk directly benefits from requires a BIP that integrates the two protocols. Integrating the two protocols means: Support for Beanstalk to compute the BDV of a given Well LP token in order to reward a corresponding amount of Stalk and Seeds upon Deposit in the Silo; Conversions to and from Beans and the Well LP token (at minimum); Support for Beanstalk to read how far above or below peg the Bean price is in a Well, such that Beanstalk can mint Beans/Soil accordingly; and Whitelisting the BEAN:ETH Well LP token. Anticipated Mayflower Timeline Last updated May 24, 2023. Late April BIP-34: Sunrise Improvements Voting Period begins BIP-35: Stalk Delegation and Process Amendments Voting Period begins Halborn and Cyfrin audits of Basin end Silo V3 audit begins Early May BIP-34 and BIP-35 Voting Periods end Basin Integration audit starts Late May Fix review for Halborn and Cyfrin audits of Basin end Early June Silo V3 audit ends Code4rena audit of Basin begins and ends Mid June BIP-36: Silo V3 Voting Period begins Late June Basin Integration audit ends BIP-36 Voting Period ends Unripe Seeds parity is launched Early July The Basin DEX and a BEAN:ETH Well is deployed BIP-37: Basin Integration Voting Period begins Mid July BIP-37 Voting Period ends BEAN:ETH Well becomes whitelisted in the Silo
